lesson.title: Chains Within Chains: Handling Multiple Layers
lesson.summary: Some functions nest three or more layers deep, and differentiating them means applying the chain rule repeatedly from the outside in, multiplying a new derivative factor at every layer.
lesson.body:
Not every composition has just two layers. A function can be built as an outer operation wrapped around a middle operation wrapped around an innermost expression, and differentiating it requires applying the chain rule once for each layer, working from the outside inward, the same way the inside function and outside function sections practiced identifying just one layer at a time. For y = f(g(h(x))), the general pattern extends naturally: dy/dx = f'(g(h(x))) times g'(h(x)) times h'(x), a product of one derivative factor contributed by each layer.

Consider y = ln((x^2 + 1)^3), which has three layers: the outermost operation is the natural logarithm, the middle operation is cubing, and the innermost expression is the polynomial x^2 + 1. Label the middle layer h(x) = (x^2 + 1)^3 for convenience. Differentiating h itself needs the chain rule once, with outer function u^3 and inner function x^2 + 1: h'(x) = 3(x^2 + 1)^2 times 2x = 6x(x^2 + 1)^2.

Now apply the outermost logarithm layer. With f(v) = ln v, f'(v) = 1/v, evaluated at v = h(x) = (x^2 + 1)^3. The full nested chain rule gives dy/dx = f'(h(x)) times h'(x) = [1 / (x^2 + 1)^3] times 6x(x^2 + 1)^2. The (x^2 + 1)^2 in the numerator cancels two of the three factors of (x^2 + 1) in the denominator, leaving dy/dx = 6x / (x^2 + 1).

This particular example offers a built in check, using the simplifying first strategy from earlier in this chapter. The logarithm power property says ln(u^3) = 3 ln u, so before differentiating at all, y = ln((x^2 + 1)^3) can be rewritten as y = 3 ln(x^2 + 1). Differentiating this simplified two layer version needs only one application of the chain rule: dy/dx = 3 times (1 / (x^2 + 1)) times 2x = 6x / (x^2 + 1). Both the fully nested computation and the simplified shortcut agree exactly, confirming the layered derivative was assembled correctly.

Not every nested composition has such a convenient shortcut. Differentiate y = e^((x^3 + 2x)^2), which has an exponential outer layer wrapped around a squared middle layer wrapped around a polynomial innermost piece. The middle layer w(x) = (x^3 + 2x)^2 differentiates by its own chain rule as w'(x) = 2(x^3 + 2x)(3x^2 + 2). The outer exponential contributes a factor of itself, e^w. Multiplying every layer together gives dy/dx = e^((x^3 + 2x)^2) times 2(x^3 + 2x)(3x^2 + 2), with no algebraic shortcut available to simplify it further.

The discipline that makes nested compositions manageable is exactly what the inside function and outside function sections practiced separately: work from the outside in, write down each layer's own local derivative one at a time, always evaluate an outer derivative at the correct inner expression rather than differentiating it directly, and only multiply every layer's contribution together at the very end.
